title: Courtroom dramas, clipped and shared
author: Aaratrika Bhaumik
content_html:
From her room in a town in Assam, Tanisha Som, 24, would spend hours watching courtrooms, hundreds of kilometres away, come to life on her screen. She would watch women lawyers command the courtroom, threading their arguments through a thicket of questions from the Bench, pressing an argument here and conceding there, until even the most sceptical judges began to come around.

At the time, becoming a lawyer seemed a dream. She had little sense of what went on behind the soaring columns and heavy wooden doors of an institution that seemed built as much to inspire awe as to keep outsiders out.

Then, in 2022, the Supreme Court began live-streaming proceedings before its Constitutional Benches. These Benches comprise five or more judges deciding substantial questions concerning the interpretation of the Constitution.

“Until then, much of what I knew about courtrooms came from Bollywood movies. Live-streamed proceedings and courtroom clips gave me a window into how courts actually function. For the first time, I could picture myself on the other side of the screen — inside one of those courtrooms, in a black robe,” she says.

Nearly three years ago, Som made it to her dream law school. Despite the gruelling schedule of a national law university, court proceedings remained a part of her day. She would sit through Constitution Bench hearings on YouTube or stumble upon courtroom clips on Instagram, wedged between memes and viral dance trends.

“These video clips instilled in me a passion for advocacy and helped me understand courtcraft. It is not something you can really learn within the four walls of a classroom,” she says.

But the clips that gave Som an early glimpse into the profession are now at the centre of a larger debate: while they have brought transparency and scrutiny to courtrooms, exchanges between judges and lawyers can also be clipped out of context and circulated for sensationalism.

Harshita Grover, a journalist, recently moved the Supreme Court asking for restrictions on circulation of courtroom clips on digital platforms. She pointed out that many were distorted and stripped of context.

On July 24, the Supreme Court, in an interim order, barred the use and circulation of audio and video clips of judicial proceedings on social media and other digital platforms without prior permission from court registrars.

A Bench led by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant said “isolated excerpts” risked “trivialising” the administration of justice. The next hearing of the case is scheduled for September 18.

The court later clarified that “recognised news outlets” could continue reporting on proceedings, but could not “utilise” audio or video clips. However, it did not define the term “recognised news outlets”, leaving some confusion among those who report on court proceedings, especially independent journalists. While it considers a broader protocol, the court has added other stakeholders to the proceedings. These include High Courts and social media intermediaries, including Meta, LinkedIn, and X Corp.

The unfettered access Som enjoyed was elusive when Swapnil Tripathi, 29, was a law student nearly eight years ago. While interning with a Supreme Court lawyer, he spent weeks working on a case of constitutional importance, only to miss the hearing because interns were allowed inside the court only on certain days to prevent overcrowding.

“I was very disheartened. I had worked closely on the case and wanted to see how the arguments played out,” he recalls. But conversations with litigants soon made him realise that the institutional barriers to accessing courtrooms were not limited to law students. “Litigants would travel to Delhi from remote corners of the country, often for cases that could alter the course of their lives. Yet, many could not even enter the courtroom because of overcrowding,” he says.

Tripathi soon moved the Supreme Court seeking live-streaming of cases of constitutional importance. In September 2018, his petition culminated in a landmark ruling recognising live-streaming as part of the right to access justice under Article 21 of the Constitution. Underlining that “sunlight is the best disinfectant”, Justice D.Y. Chandrachud reasoned that the public’s right to know how justice is administered is integral to a functioning democracy. The court also urged High Courts to gradually introduce live-streaming while framing rules to govern its use.

Letting the sunlight in

In March 2026, Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal told the Lok Sabha that live-streaming was operational in 11 High Courts. The Supreme Court’s official YouTube channel has now amassed over 2.67 lakh subscribers, with major Constitution Bench proceedings available to anyone with a screen and an Internet connection. A video of its suo motu hearing in the R.G. Kar rape-murder case, uploaded in September 2024, has been viewed nearly 48,000 times — an audience that could never have squeezed into a physical courtroom. This is one of the rare instances when a rape case was live-streamed on the apex court’s YouTube channel.

Although the Supreme Court has 17 functioning courtrooms, it largely live-streams only Constitution Bench hearings, which are held intermittently. In contrast, High Courts such as Gujarat, Karnataka, and Calcutta live-stream proceedings daily from a majority of their courtrooms. Gujarat became the first High Court to formally go live on YouTube in July 2021 and its channel now has nearly 1.97 lakh subscribers.

Also Read : Delhi HC orders action after obscene content disrupts virtual hearing

Live streams are not the only source of courtroom footage online. The Supreme Court and High Courts also allow lawyers and litigants to join hearings virtually through platforms such as Cisco Webex, with links often made available through daily cause lists. Clips from these proceedings, too, have found their way onto social media, including from sensitive matters involving sexual offences, matrimonial disputes, and child custody.

Tripathi, who now heads Charkha (Centre for Constitutional Law) at the Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy, a think tank, says the 2018 judgment anticipated some of the concerns being flagged today. “Safeguards were built in from the beginning,” he says, pointing out that matrimonial and sexual assault cases and proceedings involving children and juveniles were excluded from live-streaming. The Supreme Court e-Committee’s Model Rules released in 2021, he notes, also prohibit unauthorised dissemination and use of courtroom footage for commercial, promotional, or advertising purposes. “However, what we are seeing now is that virtual hearing links are often shared indiscriminately beyond litigants and lawyers,” he says.

“So even when High Courts pause live-streaming for sensitive cases, people logged into the virtual hearing can record the proceedings and put them on social media despite rules prohibiting unauthorised recording,” he adds.

Anjali Bhardwaj, activist and co-convener of the National Campaign for People’s Right to Information | Photo Credit: The Hindu

Anjali Bhardwaj, activist and co-convener of the National Campaign for People’s Right to Information, says the interim order marks a shift towards a permission regime. “Requiring ordinary citizens to seek permission from court registrars to share or disseminate proceedings that are otherwise live-streamed leaves room for arbitrariness,” she says. “There is no clarity on how permission is to be sought, the grounds for granting or denying it, or the recourse available if it is refused.” Acknowledging the risk of clips being taken out of context, Bhardwaj suggests that a better safeguard could be to expand live-streaming and archiving of proceedings on authorised platforms instead of restricting their circulation. “A complete, official record acts as a deterrent and allows manipulated clips to be readily exposed.”

A courtroom in your feed

A netizen may now swipe past holiday photos, influencer reels, and courtroom scenes with the same detached ease. Controversial matrimonial cases can draw over 1 lakh views. Sometimes, lawyers use a judge’s remark to leverage their social media following.

In July 2026, the Bar Council of India issued a circular prohibiting reels and promotional content from court premises. It also directed State Bar Councils to designate social media ethics nodal officers to deal with complaints and lawyers to submit a signed undertaking at the time of enrolment pledging to maintain professional conduct on social media.

“Matrimonial and custody cases generally draw the most attention on social media,” says Ravitosh Dubey, founder of legal news portal LawChakra. “Someone going through a divorce, for instance, would be curious to see how courts approach such cases, the questions judges ask, and how the process unfolds,” he says.

Since the interim order, LawChakra has largely shifted to explanatory videos without courtroom footage. Clips that accurately represent court proceedings should not be restricted, Dubey says. At LawChakra, edits were limited to trimming pauses and removing litigants’ personal details. “I have consciously refrained from publishing heated exchanges between the Bench and the Bar when, viewed in isolation, they could misrepresent what transpired in court.”

The proliferation of courtroom clips has also brought lawyers under scrutiny. They are increasingly aware that their clients may be watching. “You cannot simply seek unnecessary adjournments,” says Supreme Court advocate Lavkesh Bhambhani. “To earn your fee, you have to satisfy the client that you have done justice to their case.”

Bhambhani, however, is unfazed by the reputational risks that come with such exposure. “It is part and parcel of advocacy and you have to embrace it,” he says. “There will be good days too when an argument earns you unexpected praise from the Bench.”

Oral observations are often used to test arguments and do not necessarily reflect the reasoning or conclusions recorded in the final order, says former Supreme Court judge Abhay S. Oka. “Sometimes we question lawyers, even corner them, simply to bring out the best in them. A prima facie view expressed at the outset can change as arguments unfold,” he says.

Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul, former Supreme Court judge | Photo Credit: The Hindu

Former Supreme Court judge Sanjay Kishan Kaul cautions that the prospect of being quoted out of context on social media could make judges more circumspect. “Judges may hesitate to engage as freely with lawyers. Ultimately, it is the litigant who suffers,” he says. Kaul also points to the role of journalists in reporting court proceedings. “Court proceedings are technical in nature, which is why you need trained journalists who understand what is happening and can present the complete picture,” he says.

Holding up a mirror

In September 2024, videos of Karnataka High Court judge Justice Vedavyasachar Srishananda sparked furore online. He was seen in one video referring to a Muslim-dominated locality in west Bengaluru as “Pakistan” and making a sexist remark to a woman lawyer in another.

Within days, a Supreme Court Bench led by then CJI D.Y. Chandrachud took suo motu cognisance, cautioning judges against making “casual observations” reflecting communal bias or misogyny. The judge later apologised and the proceedings were closed. More recently, CJI Kant’s reported reference to “cockroaches” during a hearing on fake law degrees drew widespread criticism and spawned the Cockroach Janta Party, which went on to spearhead protests against examination paper leaks. CJI Kant later said his remarks had been “misquoted” by the media.

Oral observations by judges are crucial to report despite having no binding value, says Manu Sebastian, managing editor of legal news portal LiveLaw. “They offer an insight into judicial thinking and hold a mirror to the institution. The response should be introspection, not clamping down on public scrutiny or reportage,” he says.

He points to the Supreme Court’s 2021 ruling in Chief Election Commissioner vs M.R. Vijayabhaskar, which protected the reporting of oral remarks and stressed the role of public scrutiny in ensuring institutional accountability.

Sebastian adds that the exemption for “recognised news outlets” could favour established media organisations over citizen journalists and smaller newsrooms. He sees little justification for permitting written accounts of courtroom exchanges while prohibiting video clips that faithfully reproduce them.

“AI-generated or doctored videos should be prohibited. But faithful reporting, regardless of the medium, should be permitted,” he says.

The risk of misreporting, Justice Oka notes, predates the social media age. “I remember being misquoted by a trainee print journalist when I was a Bombay High Court judge,” he says.

“Oral remarks can be misreported or sensationalised in newspaper reports too. But as long as judges confine themselves to the merits of the case, that should not deter them from speaking their minds,” he adds.

Pointing to a rapidly evolving media ecosystem, legal scholar Alok Prasanna Kumar says courts must adapt to changing news consumption habits. “Allowing an oral exchange to be reported in print while restricting its dissemination through video clips is at odds with how people consume news today,” he says. “It is a bit like trying to stop the wind from blowing.”

A March 2026 report by the Reuters Institute, which facilitates programmes to promote the practice and analysis of journalism, captures the shift. It states that people in the 18 to 24 age group citing social media as their main source of news rose from 21% in 2015 to 39% in 2025, overtaking news websites and apps. The report also describes young audiences as increasingly “social-first”, with much of their news consumption incidental rather than intentional. 

Any new restrictions should follow wide-ranging consultation, says former Supreme Court judge Madan B. Lokur. “A unilateral decision is never welcome. Any institutional reform should involve all High Courts and stakeholders.”

Som, now in her final months of law school, will soon don the black robes she once dreamt of. But she remains wary of depending on traditional media to tell her what happens inside a courtroom. “The judiciary wields enormous power over our lives. I don’t want a sanitised version of how that power is exercised,” she says.

“I would rather see what happened and decide for myself.”

title: Centre willing to return unfilled NEET-SS seats to T.N. government doctors, tells Supreme Court
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
The Union government informed the Supreme Court on Thursday of its willingness to revert all the vacant National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test-Super Speciality seats (NEET-SS) for in-service government doctors to the State of Tamil Nadu.

Appearing before a Bench headed by Justice P.S. Narasimha, Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, for the Centre, submitted that the qualifying percentile for super speciality admissions would be reduced. However, the extent or quantum of such reduction has not yet been decided.

Senior Advocate P. Wilson, appearing for petitioner Tamil Nadu Medical Officers Association, stressed that the State needed to return the vacant seats, as many eligible candidates, mostly doctors serving in rural areas, were awaiting a reduction in the qualifying percentile.

In a previous hearing, the Union government had submitted that out of the 152 seats transferred by the State of Tamil Nadu, approximately 40 seats continued to remain vacant. Mr. Wilson had submitted that all 40 in-service seats must be returned to Tamil Nadu as 111 candidates were awaiting a reduction in the qualifying percentile.

The association had challenged the “premature diversion” of 152 vacant Super Speciality seats earmarked for in-service government doctors in Tamil Nadu to the All India Quota. It had also sought protection of the State’s in-service reservation policy, pending a final decision on reduction of the NEET-SS qualifying percentile.

The petition has submitted that Tamil Nadu had earmarked 219 super speciality seats for in-service candidates for the academic year 2025-2026. Upon completion of two rounds of counselling, only 68 candidates had joined, leaving as many as 152 seats vacant.

“Over 111 in-service candidates remain on the waiting list and are legitimately anticipating a reduction of the qualifying percentile in accordance with the consistent practice followed during previous academic sessions.

A substantial number of these candidates narrowly missed the existing qualifying percentile and would become eligible if the qualifying percentile is reduced/relaxed,” the association said.

The court listed the case next on September 8 to hear from the Centre the extent of reduction in the qualifying percentile.

title: Report warns against bid to privatise Employees’ State Insurance Corporation
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
ESI Ki Baat, a report on the functioning of Employees’ State Insurance Corporation (ESIC) prepared by Safe In India, a non-profit organisation, has warned the Union government against the reported attempts to privatise the ESIC. It has also recommended that the wage ceiling to avail ESIC coverage could be increased to ₹33,000 from the present figure of ₹21,000. Releasing the report, Director General of the ESIC, Ashok Kumar Singh, said the implementation of the Code on Social Security would help in more number of workers availing the ESIC benefits.

Mr. Singh said the number of beneficiaries wa growing very fast and the ESIC was creating a digital system where human interference was less so that the whole process could be based on rules. He said Panchdeep 2.0, an upgraded digital platform engineered to scale healthcare and cash benefit services seamlessly nationwide, would soon be rolled out. On implementing the Social Security Code and the expansion of ESIC’s ambit, he said the definition of the establishment and workers was so wide that even farmers could be included into the social security network. “So, there is a big responsibility on the shoulders of the government. We are supporting the government to arrive at a suitable scheme for the gig and platform workers,” he added.

The report said private involvement should be permitted only where there was demonstrated evidence of improved outcomes for workers, employers, or the ESIC, and only where the ESIC retained control, set the rules, and could reverse the arrangement. “Privatisation as a default or ideological position is counter-productive,” it said.

Global experience

The report said healthcare privatisation functioned only where regulatory capacity was sufficient to enforce standards, prevent cream-skimming, and hold private providers accountable. “Any reform proposal that depends on the private sector must demonstrate how regulation will be designed, enforced, and sustained,” it added, and urged the government that proposed reforms must learn from international experience.

C. V. Anand, others praise The Hindu’s journey of credible journalism, recall long standing association
author: P. Laxma Reddy
content_html:
“I remember sitting on the footpath outside The Hindu’s Begumpet office in 1992, to check if my name featured in the UPSC results that were displayed on a notice board there, along with the many aspirants who thronged the place. With a lot of anxiety, I searched for my name. After a anxious search I found I had secured the 147th rank. I was so relieved that I sat there for some time,” Director General of Police (DGP) C.V. Anand said, recalling a cherished moment in his long association with the newspaper.

Hyderabad 50yrs Logo Inside

The DGP lauded the newspaper’s editorial-page articles and in-depth reports, while speaking as chief guest at the celebrations of 50 years of prining in Hyderabad of The Hindu, at the paper’s office here on Thursday. He praised the newspaper for its contribution to informed public discourse and its commitment to accuracy, editorial integrity, and analytical reporting.

A former cricketer Mr. Anand said he began reading The Hindu at the age of eight with sports news and has continued to read the newspaper ever since.

“You (The Hindu) have always kept pace with change, not only in terms of technology but also in design, without compromising your values,” he said, adding that the newspaper had played a significant role in shaping his personality.

He commended The Hindu for its exclusive reports on major incidents that had changed the course of the nation and said its accurate reporting had helped governments in nation-building.

Director General of Police C. V. Anand shares a piece of cake with The Hindu Resident Editor Telangana M. Ravi Reddy at the celebrations. Also seen are I&PR Commissioner Mukund Reddy, media advisor to CM Karri Sriram, CPRO to CM G. Malsur, Senior General Manager Advertisement P Srikanth, Political Editor R. Ravikanth Reddy, General Manager S. D. T. Rao, News Editor (AP and TG)  Dinesh Akki, Chief of Bureau Serish Nanisetti, Resident Editor The Hindu Businessline Richa Mishra. | Photo Credit: NAGARA GOPAL

Commissioner of Information and Public Relations (I&PR) G. Mukunda Reddy recalled how reading The Hindu had helped him prepare for and clear the Group-I examination. The newspaper continued to provide abundant information for aspirants preparing for competitive examinations, particularly the UPSC and State public service examinations, he noted.

Describing The Hindu as an ‘extraordinary institution’, Media Adviser to the Chief Minister Karri Sriram praised the paper for several pioneering initiatives, including the use of an aircraft to transport newspapers, and commended the newspaper for its accurate and in-depth coverage on government’s policies and projects like HYDRAA and the Musi rejuvenation project.

Chief Public Relations Officer (CPRO) in the Chief Minister’s Office G. Malsur also recalled his admiration for the newspaper’s credible reporting.

The DGP and other guests unveiled a special supplement brought out by The Hindu’s Hyderabad edition. Resident Editor Telangana Ravi Reddy and General Manager, The Hindu, Hyderabad, S. D. T. Rao explained the newspaper’s commitment to journalistic values. Resident Editor, The Hindu Business Line, Richa Mishra, Chief of Bureau, The Hindu, Serish Nanisetti, Political Editor R. Ravikanth Reddy, News Editor Dinesh Akki, and Senior General Manager Pittala Srikanth were present.

title: Arts of combat: Keralites try their hand at new martial arts
author: Tiki Rajwi
content_html:
There is a moment in the 2023 Marko Zaror-starrer Chilean martial arts flick The Fist of the Condor (El puño del condor) where the antagonist, played by Eyal Meyer, leaps high in the thick of a fight, twists his outstretched body mid-flight and drops into a neat Ashwa Vadivu. Kalaripayattu practitioners will quickly identify the ‘horse stance’ as something singular to their art. But Chile in Andean South America is scarcely a place one instantly associates with the move.

“I had received a phone call from Marko, saying they were making a new movie and wanted to introduce different martial arts and techniques to the project. He had heard about me as an actor and my relationship with Kalaripayattu. He told me that we should first rehearse to see if this martial art would work for the movie.I immediately said, 'Sure, let’s go for it,'”Meyer, who first came into contact with the martial art in 2006 while studying acting and theatre at the University of Chile, told The Hindu in a recent e-mail interview. Today, the actor runs Mauna Kalari in Santiago, the Chilean capital.

Back at home

While Kalaripayattu has been making ripples across the globe, back home in Keralam, its birthplace, a different kind of revolution is taking place on the local martial arts scene.

A sparring session in progress at the JB Fit Club in Thiruvananthapuram. | Photo Credit: Jayamohan A.

In State capital Thiruvananthapuram, 19-year-old Muhammed Aiman S. plans to launch a rigorous three-month preparation soon for Sanda, a Chinese full-contact sport, for the University Games in December. Before the advent of the internet and social media, very few people would have heard of this sport. Now Sanda is a staple of the thriving combat sport environment in Keralam along with Mixed Martial Arts (MMA), Muay Thai and Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu (BJJ). “I will have two training sessions daily— one each in the morning and evening. Sanda is a speed game, with punches, kicks and take-downs,” explains Aiman, who fights out of the Johny Brothers Fight Club. A regular on the Muay Thai, Kickboxing and Sanda fight circuit, the psychology undergraduate began training in combat sports at a young age, amassing medals in the sub-junior and junior categories at the State and national levels. He recently won two of his three pro fights.

Win in Thailand

Ann Mary Philip from Edapally, Kochi, came to combat sports in her late thirties and went on to score a win in Thailand, the home of Muay Thai. Ann encountered kickboxing in 2018 while searching for a class for her son, Chris. Over the years, under the guidance of her coach Kiran V.S. of SpaRing combat sports gym, Ann evolved into Muay Thai, Boxing and the Russian combat sport of Sambo. At 42, she has now started training in BJJ. She first took part in a boxing tournament in 2024 when she was turning 40. “Forty is the age limit for amateur matches, but I had this great desire to experience boxing at least once. So my debut match was also my retirement match,” says Ann, who is a certified referee in Sambo and secretary general of the Sambo India Association.

People like Aiman and Ann represent the new breed of combat sports enthusiasts in the land of Kalaripayattu. Till a few years ago, the traditional martial arts (TMA) scene in Keralam was restricted to the big ‘Ks’— Karate, Kalaripayattu and Kung Fu— with Korean Taekwondo making a big entrance later on with its Olympic-sport tag. Today, MMA and Muay Thai clubs are all the rage in cities like Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram and Kozhikode and smaller towns, courtesy social media and YouTube. Unlike Karate classes of the 1980s or 1990s, which were usually conducted twice or thrice a week in school auditoriums after class hours or atop the roof of somebody’s house, today it is all about snazzy-looking gyms with floor mats, protective gear, weight racks, boxing rings and a bevy of heavy bags lining the wall for punching and kicking.

“MMA is by far the most popular because of the Ultimate Fighting Championship,” says Joys Varghese, founder of Spartans Martial Arts and Fitness. A recognised referee in combat sport events such as MMA and Muay Thai, he himself had begun his martial arts journey with Karate. Joys says he switched to MMA because he wanted something practical and would work in a real-life scenario. “Youngsters today are not interested in spending time on the forms (set routines) in Karate and Kung-Fu. They want faster, workable results,” says Joys.

Combat sport gyms

In these new combat sport gyms across Keralam, the emphasis is on what works inside the octagonal MMA cage, the boxing ring or on the mat. The romance of Shaolin Temple-inspired spiritual quests through martial arts takes a back seat here. Television and social media platforms dedicated to combat sports have played a big role in encouraging the younger generation to try out and even pursue careers in these money-spinning sports.

MMA is precisely what the name suggests: an eclectic mixture of punches, kicks, knees, elbows, wrestling takedowns, locks and chokes. Muay Thai, the art of eight limbs, first caught the imagination of Indian youth through movies of Thai star Tony Jaa. Real-life fighters such as Saenchai, Buakaw Banchamek, Tawanchai and Rodtang Jitmuangnon, who enjoy a global following, are as familiar to combat sport buffs in today’s Keralam as the legendary figures of Kalaripayattu lore, Thacholi Othenan or Aromal Chekavar.

“Social media is the biggest reason for Muay Thai (or Thai Boxing) becoming so popular today,” says Binu Joseph, president of the Kerala State Muay Thai Association.

Binu had started training in Muay Thai in 2009 in Bengaluru. “I was already doing Karate and Kickboxing at the time. In 2014, we conducted the first Muay Thai refereeing seminar at Kalikavu in Malappuram district. Coaches from nine districts participated in it. Today, Muay Thai is one of two combat sports that are in high demand among youth in Keralam, the other being MMA,” he says. The association was also formed the same year. “Before social media, people here did not have much awareness about martial arts beyond Karate, Kalari or Kung Fu. That is not the case nowadays. They know about other sports that are effective and engaging,” he observes.

To train at clubs abroad

With the world becoming smaller, Keralites are also increasingly travelling to places such as Thailand and Japan to train at clubs there. Binu himself has been to Thailand twice. Ann went to Thailand in 2024 to attend a camp. “They have fight nights every week. I registered, and I got a Muay Thai bout at the Bangla stadium which I won in the minus-50 category,” says Ann.

Keralites’ craze for martial arts is nothing new. The history of Kalaripayattu goes back centuries. The post-Independence years of the 20th century saw a revival of interest in it, thanks to the efforts of teachers such as C.V. Narayanan Nair and Chirakkal T. Sreedharan Nair. How the current influx of foreign combat arts would influence Kalaripayattu remains to be seen.

In the late 1970s, Karate came to Keralam with a big bang, riding on the excitement generated by Bruce Lee’s 1973 movie Enter the Dragon. Notably, the Japanese martial art made its entrance not directly from Japan but via Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka. “Those days, youngsters studied Karate in secret, as parents tended to frown upon it. Today, they are more receptive,” says K. Nagulanathan, who teaches the Shotokan style of Karate in Thrissur. Nagulanathan had come to Keralam from Kilinochchi in Sri Lanka in 1981 and settled here to teach Karate. He does not believe that the entry of sports such as MMA has displaced Karate. The number of students has, in fact, increased, although their aspirations have changed, he says.

But this is where things get really interesting. In the midst of this martial arts ‘outbreak,’ there is also heightened interest in Kalaripayattu in its homeland.

“There is a revival. During a visit to Bengaluru, I was astonished to see the number of people taking up Kalaripayattu. People are also more aware about Kalaripayattu’s influence on other art forms,” says S.R.D. Prasad, an octogenarian Gurukkal (senior trainer), who runs the Sree Bharath Kalari at Valapattanam, Kannur. His father Chirakkal Sreedharan Nair had established the Kalari in 1948. The renewed interest, he says, is due to many factors, not least the Union government picking Kalaripayattu veterans for the coveted Padma Awards. Recipients include Meenakshi Amma, Sankara Narayana Menon Chundayil and Prasad himself. Prasad adds that Kalaripayattu teachers have also been forced to adapt to changing requirements.

Renewed interest in Kalaripayattu

In Thiruvananthapuram, the CVN Kalari continues to be a go-to place for Kalaripayattu enthusiasts. G. Sathyanarayanan,the grandson of C.V. Narayanan Nair, concurs that there is a renewed interest in Kalaripayattu. “A lot of the interest in Kalari is fuelled by the internet,” he notes. While changing times indeed call for changed strategies, it is still preferable to start the training between the ages of eight and 16, says Mr. Sathyanarayanan, who is now the Gurukkal at CVN Kalari. “Because the body is still supple and Kalaripayattu is not like other sports. It is an integrated system, and the body has to be prepared for structured training.”

Chilean actorEyal Meyer during a Kalaripayattu training session. | Photo Credit: Special arrangement

Back in Chile, Meyer dreams of a sequel to The Fist of the Condor. “I hope so! I always tell Marko (Zaror) and Ernesto (Ernesto Diaz Espinoza, the film’s director) that we should do a second part that has more fighting sequences using Kalaripayattu’s weapons like the urumi. I have not seen that showcased in Western movies,” he says. Meyer has trained with the Kozhikode-based Hindustan Kalari Sangam, which he first contacted in 2008. “I finally arrived there in August 2011, where I was received openly and with warmth by everyone,” he recalls. He has since been to Keralam a number of times. He has his own take on Kalaripayattu’s prospects. “I don’t agree with the argument that it is a relic art. It is such a wise and profound technology for the body and mind that I feel it is more current than one thinks,” he notes.

Meyer has trained with the Kozhikode-based Hindustan Kalari Sangam, which he first contacted in 2008. “I finally arrived there in August 2011, where I was received openly and with warmth by everyone,” he recalls. He has since been to Keralam a number of times. He has his own take on Kalaripayattu’s prospects. “I don’t agree with the argument that it is a relic art. It is such a wise and profound technology for the body and mind that I feel it is more current than one thinks,” he notes.

title: Fading fear of HIV puts focus on rising STI risks among youth in Keralam
author: C Maya
content_html:
HIV is no longer the word that frightens young people. For a generation that has grown up seeing HIV transformed from a feared death sentence into a manageable chronic condition, the virus no longer carries the deterrent power it once did.

But the fading fear of HIV is confronting Keralam with a new public-health challenge. Changing sexual behaviour, gaps in information and awareness, and growing substance use are increasingly putting young people at risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs).

The numbers seeking care at the 23 District STI/RTI Centres (DSRCs) under the Kerala State AIDS Control Society (KSACS) have been rising steadily. However, these figures do not capture the full picture, as Keralam does not have routine STI surveillance across public and private hospitals. STIs also rarely figure in formal public-health conversations.

World Sexual Health Day

On World Sexual Health Day (September 4), experts say Keralam needs more open conversations with young people about sexual health, safe sexual practices, consent and healthy relationships. Equally important is ensuring that youngsters know where they can seek confidential testing, advice and treatment without fear of judgement.

KSACS data compiled up to December 2025 show that attendance at DSRCs rose from 41,417 in 2023-24 to 63,129 in 2024-25. Another 51,243 people visited the clinics during April-November 2025 alone.

The proportion of DSRC clients undergoing RPR screening for syphilis also increased—from 55% in 2023-24 to 70% in 2024-25 and 79% during April-November 2025. The increase in screening means more infections are being detected, and the figures cannot by themselves be taken as evidence of a corresponding rise in prevalence.

Of particular concern is the increase among younger clients. Among those aged up to 19, clinic attendance rose from 1,547 in 2023-24 to 2,255 in 2024-25; another 1,910 had been recorded during April-November 2025. The proportion of newly detected HIV infections among those aged 15-24 also rose from 10% in 2022-23 to 15% during April-October 2025.

Change in societal attitude

“There is a change in societal attitude towards casual sex and today, the earlier message of abstinence that we used to give youngsters no longer works. Many youngsters are sexually active today and our only message to them is to remain safe, because their health is at stake,” a senior Health official said.

Being safe goes beyond HIV prevention. Condoms significantly reduce the risk of many STIs, including HIV, gonorrhoea and chlamydia, but do not eliminate the risk of infections such as syphilis, HPV and genital herpes, which can spread through skin-to-skin contact. HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, regular testing, timely treatment and reducing exposure to multiple or unknown partners are also important.

Consent and communication also need to be part of sexual-health messaging. Being safe means being able to say no, respecting a partner’s decision and discussing protection before sex.

Substance use among young people is another concern for sexual-health professionals, who say intoxication can increase risky sexual behaviour and impair the ability to make informed decisions.

How crucial testing is

“One of the most important messages we can give youth today is that testing matters, even without symptoms. Many STIs cause no symptoms, so someone can have and transmit an infection without knowing it. Testing becomes particularly important after a potential exposure or when starting a new sexual relationship,” said V. Sam Prasad, who heads AHF India Cares, an NGO working in HIV.

Keralam’s STI clinics are seeing a range of infections, with syphilis emerging as a particular concern. Doctors also report a resurgence of gonorrhoea, which they say is increasingly being encountered in clinical practice.

KSACS data show that clients found reactive for syphilis on screening increased from 1,206 in 2023-24 to 1,455 in 2024-25, with another 1,121 recorded during the first seven months of 2025-26.

‘Serious complications’

“We are quite concerned that some STIs are now presenting differently and with serious complications. We have had reports of neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and cardiovascular syphilis, which are complicated and require long and intensive treatment,” a Health official said.

At STI clinics, young people diagnosed with an infection are encouraged to bring their partners for testing to prevent reinfection. They are also advised to complete treatment and undergo HIV testing, given the close relationship between HIV and other STIs.

Self-assessment tool

To encourage confidential testing, KSACS has launched a digital self-assessment tool through which users can privately assess their sexual-health risk. By scanning a QR code and answering questions about lifestyle and behavioural practices, users receive guidance on whether testing may be advisable, along with information on the next steps and the nearest STI clinic.
